blocks.text: An EEG measures the electrical activity of the brain; its principle is detecting the nerve impulses passing between neurons.

items: Procedure: metal electrodes are attached to the scalp and connected to an amplifier, which magnifies the signals; they are recorded and shown as waveforms on a screen or paper.
Uses: to evaluate seizures, epilepsy and brain tumours. It is painless and needs no sedation or anaesthesia.

blocks.alt: A head with many electrodes attached to the scalp, their wires gathered together, and beside it a sheet of wavy traces labelled EEG reading.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.22: Electroencephalography (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.22).

blocks.alt: Five EEG wave traces in coloured bands: Gamma (fastest, smallest), Beta, Alpha, Theta and Delta (slowest, largest). From gamma to delta the waves become slower and taller.
blocks.caption: EEG waves (original drawing after the waveforms in the textbook's 'For Information' box on EEG).
